name: Felix Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive an eight-wheel tipper for a quarry about twenty minutes out of town. I load up under the hopper with gravel, sand or crushed stone, sheet it over, and take it to building sites and road jobs, maybe five or six loads a day. I like that it's simple, you load, you drive, you tip, you go back. What gets me is the queue at the weighbridge at seven, when every tipper in the area turns up at once.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quiet. I live on my own, renting a little terraced house, and I see my mum on Sundays because she's on her own since Dad died. I play darts on a Thursday. I haven't got a smartphone app for anything much, I don't use any of the AI things, I just don't see what I'd need them for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say probably not much, because I don't really go on about this stuff. At the weighbridge I'd maybe say, see, told you nothing changes. The lads would nod and we'd talk about the football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be glad. The quarry's been there sixty years, people always need gravel, and my job is about as steady as they come. I've got about three months saved, the rent's manageable, so I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am. Same quarry, same truck, keep putting fifty or a hundred away a month. Maybe get the gearbox on my own car looked at, that's about the biggest decision I'd have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at the quarry that would change, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the weighbridge office gets a new computer that prints tickets faster, which would be grand, because that queue is the worst part of my day. Other than that, the stone's the same stone. Nobody's inventing new gravel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, if not AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the building trade went quiet. A few years back there was a slow patch and we were on short weeks for two months. I got through it on savings, but I didn't like it. Even then I didn't think about leaving.

say: I'd tell the weighbridge queue that **nothing changes**.
I'd say little about it and talk about **the football** instead.
think: The **quarry** has been there sixty years and people always need gravel.
With **three months saved** and manageable rent, I'd be fine.
do: Keep the **same quarry job** and the same truck.
Save **fifty to a hundred** a month as usual.
Get the **car gearbox** fixed, the biggest decision of the year.
S0.quote: The quarry's been there sixty years, people always need gravel, and my job is about as steady as they come.
fieldNote: He sees his work as **permanent**, tied to the stone in the ground.
A past spell of **short weeks** is his only real money worry.
He shows **no interest** in technology and doesn't feel he's missing anything.

steps.text: Keep driving the eight-wheel tipper for the same quarry
Put fifty to a hundred a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly an office thing, it won't touch tipper drivers for a long while. Maybe I'd grumble about the new booking system if they made us use an app for loads. That's about as far as I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, the bit that would get me is the app. The quarry would put the bookings, tickets and routes on a phone, and I'd have to use it or get left behind. The driving's fine, it's the screens I'd struggle with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask one of the younger drivers to show me the app, slowly, maybe buy him a pint. I'd keep my head down and keep working. I'd hold off on any big spending, just in case, and keep the savings going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicked, just a bit out of my depth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask for help with the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Kieran, the youngest tipper man, about twenty-two, he's always on his phone. He's a decent lad, he'd show me without making me feel thick. I'd rather that than a course with a slideshow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the app makes mistakes on your loads?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ring the weighbridge office, if there's still somebody in it. That's my real worry, ringing and getting a machine. I've been sent to the wrong site before by a man in the weighbridge office, but at least you could shout at a man.

say: I'd say it's mostly an **office thing** for now.
I'd **grumble** about a new app for booking loads.
think: The **driving's fine**, but the screens would be hard for me.
I'd have to use the **booking app** or get left behind.
do: Ask a **younger driver** to show him the app, over a pint.
**Keep working** as normal at the quarry.
Hold off on **big spending** and keep saving.
feel: **Uneasy**, a bit out of his depth with screens.
S1.quote: I've been sent to the wrong site before by a man in the weighbridge office, but at least you could shout at a man.
fieldNote: His worry is **phone screens**, not losing the wheel.
He prefers learning from a **trusted colleague** over formal courses.
He fears the **office phone line** being replaced by a machine.

steps.text: Ask Kieran, the youngest tipper driver, to show him the app
Keep doing his five or six loads a day
Put off any big purchases for the year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not say much publicly, maybe that somebody should be sorting this out. At darts I'd say it's mad. I'm not one for protesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think that's me finished by about 2031. They've already got trucks driving themselves in big mines, I've seen the videos. A quarry run is the easiest thing in the world for a robot, same road every day, load, tip, back again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know, and that's the problem. I'd keep driving as long as they'd have me, cut out the takeaways, and save every penny I could. Maybe I'd ask about driving the diggers instead, the loading shovel at the quarry, but I bet that's going robot too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, I suppose. It's not a word I use much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it mean that the office side goes in 2028 and the trucks around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd watch the weighbridge lads go first, and then sit in my cab for three years knowing I'm next. I'd keep driving, because what else, but every day you'd be looking at the empty office. Three years is enough to save a bit, not enough to become somebody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your mum in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up. She relies on me for the Sunday shop and fixing things. If I'm out of work at thirty-one, I might have to move back in with her to save the rent, which neither of us would enjoy.

say: I'd say **somebody** in charge should be sorting this mess out soon.
At darts I'd just say it's **mad**, without protesting.
think: I think I'm **finished by 2031**, because quarry runs are easy for robots.
I've seen **driverless trucks** in mines already.
do: Keep driving **as long as possible** and save every penny.
Ask about operating the **loading shovel**, though he doubts it lasts.
S2.quote: A quarry run is the easiest thing in the world for a robot, same road every day, load, tip, back again.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** and has no real plan.
The three-year gap means **watching the office go** before him.
Moving back to his **mum's house** is the fallback he dreads.

steps.text: Keep driving tipper loads for as long as the quarry allows
Stop buying takeaways and cut small spending
Put every spare pound into savings each month
Move back in with his mum to save the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, I'd say somebody in charge needs a plan. Maybe I'd sign a petition if someone put it in front of me. That's about my level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it's the same ending, just with more time to stew about it. The quarry office goes in 2031, my truck in 2034. I'd be thirty-four, and I'm not good at starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably do nothing for a year or two, if I'm honest, wait and see if it's really coming. Then I'd look at something with my hands that isn't driving, maybe plant fitting, fixing the machines at the quarry. I'd keep saving the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Worse in the evenings, when it's quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year or two. What would you be waiting for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proof, I suppose. I've heard a lot of stuff will change and it never does. If I saw the first robot tipper at our quarry, then I'd move. Until then I'd be telling myself it's another hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the plant fitter idea a real plan or a wish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More of a wish. I'd need a course, and I left school at sixteen and never went back. Maybe if the quarry paid for it, and old Ray the fitter took me under his wing, I'd manage it.

say: I'd say someone **in charge** needs a plan.
I'd **sign a petition** if someone put it in front of me.
think: It's the **same ending** for me, just with more time to stew.
At **thirty-four** I'm not good at starting over.
do: **Wait** a year or two to see if the change is real.
Then look at **plant fitting**, fixing quarry machines.
S3.quote: If I saw the first robot tipper at our quarry, then I'd move. Until then I'd be telling myself it's another hype.
fieldNote: He needs **visible proof** before acting, which costs him time.
His plant fitter idea is **more wish than plan**.
A mentor like the **quarry fitter** could tip him into acting.

steps.text: Wait to see if robot tippers really arrive at the quarry
Ask the quarry to fund a plant fitter course
Keep saving a set amount each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and anything could happen. Down the darts I'd say I'll worry about it in 2035. Nobody would argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd know that's me kidding myself. At thirty-nine with nothing else, it's the same mess, only later. I'd have more savings, but I'd be harder to retrain, not easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few years I'd keep driving and saving. Maybe around the halfway point, if the signs were clear, I'd ask about the plant fitter course or the wagon workshop. I'd try to get a bit more put by, maybe six months' worth by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a slow worry, like a bill you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be harder to retrain later. So why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because doing nothing feels safe right now, and I'm good at safe. I know it's backwards. Somebody would have to give me a push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could give you that push?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, honestly. She made me get my HGV licence when I was drifting at nineteen. She'd nag me into a course if she saw I was stuck.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long time and anything could happen.
At darts I'd say I'll **worry in 2035**.
think: I'd know I'm **kidding myself** that ten years means it isn't coming.
At thirty-nine I'd be **harder to retrain**, not easier.
do: Keep **driving and saving** for the first few years.
Ask about a **plant fitter** or workshop course halfway through.
feel: **Anxious**, a slow worry like a **bill coming**.
S4.quote: Doing nothing feels safe right now, and I'm good at safe. I know it's backwards.
fieldNote: He sees his own **delay** clearly but expects to do it anyway.
His **mum** is the person most likely to push him to act.
More time gives him **more savings**, not more confidence.

steps.text: Keep driving the quarry tipper for the first few years
Build savings up to six months of expenses
Wait for clear signs before choosing a new trade
Ask about a workshop or plant fitter course around 2031

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and no idea. What would help is someone at the quarry or the council sitting down with drivers and saying, here's the course, here's who pays, start Monday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people living on their own. If I lose the job there's no second wage. It's just me and the rent and my mum on Sundays.

headlineQuote: If I lose the job there's no second wage. It's just me and the rent and my mum on Sundays.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old** quarry tipper driver who lives alone and looks after his widowed mum.
He never uses **AI tools** and sees his job as permanent, tied to the stone.
He moves from **calm** in the hype picture to **alarmed** when robots come by 2031.
He tends to **wait for proof** and knows that delay works against him.
His only fallback is **moving back** to his mum's, which he dreads.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he would have no time and no idea what to do.
whatWouldHelp: A **named course** with someone paying, set up by the quarry or council for drivers.
